prompt:
The symbols $(a,b,\ldots,g)$ and $[a,b,\ldots,g]$ denote the greatest common divisor and least common multiple, respectively, of the positive integers $a,b,\ldots,g$. For example, $(3,6,18)=3$ and $[6,15]=30$. Prove that
$$\frac{[a,b,c]^2}{[a,b][b,c][c,a]}=\frac{(a,b,c)^2}{(a,b)(b,c)(c,a)}.$$
answer: Compare exponents of each prime: with $\alpha\le\beta\le\gamma$ the exponents of $p$ in $a,b,c$ (in some order), both sides have exponent $-\beta$.

solutions.title: Compare prime exponents
solutions.body:
Two positive rationals are equal if every prime $p$ appears with the same exponent in both. Fix a prime $p$ and let $x, y, z \ge 0$ be the exponents of $p$ in $a, b, c$. Both sides are symmetric in $a, b, c$ (each is unchanged by any permutation of $a,b,c$), so we may relabel and assume $x \le y \le z$.

The exponent of $p$ in a gcd is the minimum of the exponents, and in an lcm the maximum. So:

- In $[a,b,c]^2$: $2z$. In $[a,b][b,c][c,a]$: $\max(x,y)+\max(y,z)+\max(z,x) = y + z + z$. The left side has exponent $2z - (y+2z) = -y$.
- In $(a,b,c)^2$: $2x$. In $(a,b)(b,c)(c,a)$: $\min(x,y)+\min(y,z)+\min(z,x) = x + y + x$. The right side has exponent $2x - (2x+y) = -y$.

The exponents agree for every prime, so the two sides are equal. ∎

solutions.title: Via the inclusion–exclusion identity
solutions.body:
For two numbers, $[u,v](u,v) = uv$. For a prime $p$ with exponents $x\le y\le z$ in $a,b,c$ (after relabelling), the exponent of $p$ in $\dfrac{abc\,(a,b,c)}{(a,b)(b,c)(c,a)}$ is $(x+y+z) + x - (x + y + x) = z$, which is the exponent in $[a,b,c]$. Hence
$$[a,b,c] = \frac{abc\,(a,b,c)}{(a,b)(b,c)(c,a)}.$$
Square it and divide by $[a,b][b,c][c,a] = \dfrac{ab\cdot bc\cdot ca}{(a,b)(b,c)(c,a)} = \dfrac{(abc)^2}{(a,b)(b,c)(c,a)}$:
$$\frac{[a,b,c]^2}{[a,b][b,c][c,a]} = \frac{(abc)^2 (a,b,c)^2}{\big((a,b)(b,c)(c,a)\big)^2}\cdot\frac{(a,b)(b,c)(c,a)}{(abc)^2} = \frac{(a,b,c)^2}{(a,b)(b,c)(c,a)}. \;∎$$

prompt: A given tetrahedron $ABCD$ is isosceles, that is, $AB=CD$, $AC=BD$, $AD=BC$. Show that the faces of the tetrahedron are acute-angled triangles.
answer: For every edge $XY$ with midpoint $M$ and opposite vertices $Z,W$: the medians $ZM, WM$ are equal, and $ZW<ZM+MW$ gives $ZM>\tfrac12 XY$, so $\angle XZY$ is acute.

solutions.title: Medians to a common edge
solutions.body:
**Key identity.** For any triangle $XZY$ with $M$ the midpoint of $XY$,
$$\vec{ZX}\cdot\vec{ZY} = (\vec{ZM}+\vec{MX})\cdot(\vec{ZM}-\vec{MX}) = ZM^2 - \tfrac14 XY^2,$$
since $\vec{MY} = -\vec{MX}$. So $\angle XZY$ is acute iff $ZM > \tfrac12 XY$.

Every angle of every face has the form $\angle XZY$ where $XY$ is an edge and $Z$ is one of the two other vertices; call the fourth vertex $W$. The edge $ZW$ is the edge opposite $XY$, so $ZW = XY$. Also the edges $XZ$ and $YW$ are opposite, as are $YZ$ and $XW$; hence $XZ = YW$ and $YZ = XW$. Thus triangles $XYZ$ and $YXW$ are congruent (SSS) by the correspondence $X\to Y$, $Y \to X$, $Z\to W$, which maps the midpoint $M$ of $XY$ to itself. Therefore the medians are equal: $ZM = WM$.

Now $Z, M, W$ are not collinear: otherwise $Z$ and $W$ would lie on a line through $M \in XY$, so all four vertices would lie in one plane, contradicting that $ABCD$ is a tetrahedron. By the strict triangle inequality in triangle $ZMW$,
$$XY = ZW < ZM + MW = 2ZM,$$
so $ZM > \tfrac12 XY$, and by the key identity $\angle XZY$ is acute.

Since this holds for every angle of every face, all faces are acute-angled. ∎

solutions.title: Vectors from one vertex
solutions.body:
Put $D$ at the origin and let $\vec a = \vec{DA}$, $\vec b = \vec{DB}$, $\vec c = \vec{DC}$. The conditions $BC = AD$, $AC = BD$, $AB = CD$ read
$$|\vec b-\vec c|^2 = |\vec a|^2,\quad |\vec a-\vec c|^2 = |\vec b|^2,\quad |\vec a-\vec b|^2 = |\vec c|^2.$$
Expanding the first: $2\,\vec b\cdot\vec c = |\vec b|^2 + |\vec c|^2 - |\vec a|^2$, and similarly for the others. Hence
$$2\,\vec b\cdot \vec c = |\vec b|^2+|\vec c|^2-|\vec a|^2 \quad\text{etc.}$$
Now compute $|\vec b + \vec c - \vec a|^2 = |\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2+|\vec c|^2 + 2\vec b\cdot\vec c - 2\vec a\cdot\vec b - 2\vec a\cdot\vec c$. Substituting the three expressions gives $|\vec b+\vec c-\vec a|^2 = 4\,\vec b\cdot\vec c$. The vector $\vec b+\vec c-\vec a$ is nonzero, because $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are linearly independent (the tetrahedron is non-degenerate). Hence $\vec b\cdot\vec c > 0$, i.e. $\angle BDC$ is acute. By symmetry $\angle ADB$ and $\angle ADC$ are acute, so all angles at $D$ are acute; the same argument at each vertex shows every face angle is acute. ∎

prompt: A random number selector can only select one of the nine integers $1, 2, \ldots, 9$, and it makes these selections with equal probability. Determine the probability that after $n$ selections ($n>1$), the product of the $n$ numbers selected will be divisible by $10$.

solutions.title: Complement and inclusion–exclusion
solutions.body:
The product is divisible by $10$ iff at least one selected number is $5$ (the only multiple of $5$ available) and at least one is even.

Let $F$ = "no 5 is chosen" and $G$ = "no even number is chosen". The product fails to be divisible by $10$ exactly on $F\cup G$.

- $P(F) = (8/9)^n$ (each selection avoids 5).
- $P(G) = (5/9)^n$ (each selection is one of $1,3,5,7,9$).
- $P(F\cap G) = (4/9)^n$ (each selection is one of $1,3,7,9$).

By inclusion–exclusion, $P(F\cup G) = (8/9)^n + (5/9)^n - (4/9)^n$, so
$$P(10 \mid \text{product}) = 1 - \left(\tfrac89\right)^n - \left(\tfrac59\right)^n + \left(\tfrac49\right)^n = \frac{9^n-8^n-5^n+4^n}{9^n}.$$
(Check $n = 2$: $(81-64-25+16)/81 = 8/81$; indeed the good ordered pairs are $(5, \text{even})$ and $(\text{even}, 5)$: $2\cdot 4 = 8$.)

solutions.title: Count the favourable sequences directly
solutions.body: Count sequences of length $n$ from $\{1,\dots,9\}$ containing at least one $5$ and at least one even number. Total $9^n$. Sequences with no $5$: $8^n$. Sequences with no even number: $5^n$. Sequences with neither: $4^n$ (from $\{1,3,7,9\}$). The favourable count is $9^n - 8^n - 5^n + 4^n$, giving probability $\dfrac{9^n-8^n-5^n+4^n}{9^n}$.

prompt:
Let $R$ denote a non-negative rational number. Determine a fixed set of integers $a,b,c,d,e,f$, such that for every choice of $R$,
$$\left|\frac{aR^2+bR+c}{dR^2+eR+f}-\sqrt[3]{2}\right|<|R-\sqrt[3]{2}|.$$
answer: For example $(a,b,c,d,e,f) = (0,2,2,1,0,2)$, i.e. $\dfrac{2R+2}{R^2+2}$. (Any choice must satisfy $e=a$, $f=b$, $c=2d$.)

solutions.title: Factor out $R - \sqrt[3]{2}$
solutions.body:
Let $t = \sqrt[3]{2}$, so $t^3 = 2$ and $2/t = t^2$.

**Finding the form.** If the inequality holds for all non-negative rationals $R$, then letting $R \to t$ through rationals forces the fraction to tend to $t$; this suggests choosing coefficients so that $R=t$ is a root of $aR^2+bR+c - t(dR^2+eR+f)$. Take $e = a$, $f = b$, $c = 2d$. Then
$$aR^2 + bR + 2d - t(dR^2 + aR + b) = (a - td)R^2 + (b - ta)R + (2d - tb),$$
and at $R=t$ this equals $at^2 - 2d + bt - at^2 + 2d - bt = 0$. Dividing by $R - t$:
$$(a-td)R^2 + (b-ta)R + (2d-tb) = (R-t)\big((a-td)R + (b - dt^2)\big)$$
(check the constant term: $-t(b - dt^2) = -tb + dt^3 = 2d - tb$ ✓).

**A concrete choice.** Take $a = 0$, $b = 2$, $d = 1$, so $c = 2$, $e = 0$, $f = 2$:
$$\frac{2R+2}{R^2+2} - t = \frac{(R-t)(-tR + 2 - t^2)}{R^2+2}.$$
So we need, for $R\ge 0$ rational,
$$|tR + t^2 - 2| < R^2 + 2. \tag{$*$}$$
(The case $R = t$ cannot occur since $t$ is irrational, so $|R-t| > 0$ and $(*)$ is exactly what is needed after dividing by $|R-t|$.)

- $tR + t^2 - 2 < R^2 + 2 \iff R^2 - tR + (4 - t^2) > 0$. This quadratic in $R$ has discriminant $t^2 - 4(4-t^2) = 5t^2 - 16 < 0$, since $t^2 = \sqrt[3]{4} < 2 < 16/5$. So it is always positive.
- $-(tR + t^2 - 2) < R^2 + 2 \iff R^2 + tR + t^2 > 0$, true for $R \ge 0$.

Hence $(*)$ holds, and
$$\left|\frac{2R+2}{R^2+2} - \sqrt[3]{2}\right| = |R - \sqrt[3]{2}|\cdot\frac{|tR+t^2-2|}{R^2+2} < |R-\sqrt[3]{2}|$$
for every non-negative rational $R$.

**Answer:** $a=0,\ b=2,\ c=2,\ d=1,\ e=0,\ f=2$. ∎

prompt: A given convex pentagon $ABCDE$ has the property that the area of each of the five triangles $ABC$, $BCD$, $CDE$, $DEA$, and $EAB$ is unity. Show that all pentagons with the above property have the same area, and calculate that area. Show, furthermore, that there are infinitely many non-congruent pentagons having the above area property.
answer: The area is always $\dfrac{5+\sqrt5}{2}$ (each diagonal is parallel to a side; with $P = BD\cap CE$, $ABPE$ is a parallelogram and $[PCD]=y$ satisfies $(1-y)^2=y$). Area-preserving affine images of a regular pentagon give infinitely many examples.

solutions.title: Parallel diagonals and a parallelogram
solutions.body:
**Each diagonal is parallel to a side.** Since $[EAB] = [ABC]$, the points $E$ and $C$ are at the same distance from line $AB$, and by convexity they lie on the same side of it; hence $EC \parallel AB$. In the same way every diagonal is parallel to the "opposite" side; in particular $BD \parallel AE$ (from $[DEA] = [EAB]$, $D$ and $B$ are equidistant from $AE$).

**The parallelogram.** Let $P$ be the intersection of the diagonals $BD$ and $CE$ (they cross inside the convex quadrilateral $BCDE$). Since $P$ lies on $EC \parallel AB$ and on $BD\parallel AE$, the quadrilateral $ABPE$ has $AB \parallel PE$ and $AE \parallel BP$, so it is a parallelogram. Its diagonal $BE$ halves it, so
$$[ABPE] = 2[ABE] = 2, \qquad [BPE] = 1.$$

**The small triangles.** Let $y = [PCD]$. From $[BCD] = [BCP] + [PCD] = 1$ and $[CDE] = [PCD] + [PDE] = 1$, we get $[BCP] = [PDE] = 1 - y$. In quadrilateral $BCDE$ with diagonals meeting at $P$, triangles with a common height give
$$\frac{[BPC]}{[CPD]} = \frac{BP}{PD} = \frac{[BPE]}{[EPD]},$$
so $[BPC]\cdot[EPD] = [CPD]\cdot[BPE]$, i.e. $(1-y)^2 = y\cdot 1$. Thus $y^2 - 3y + 1 = 0$, and since $0 < y < 1$, $y = \dfrac{3-\sqrt5}{2}$.

**The area.** Splitting the pentagon from $P$:
$$[ABCDE] = [ABPE] + [BCP] + [PCD] + [PDE] = 2 + 2(1-y) + y = 4 - y = \frac{5+\sqrt5}{2}.$$
This value does not depend on the pentagon, as required.

**Infinitely many examples.** A regular pentagon has all five triangles $ABC, \dots, EAB$ congruent, hence of equal area; scale it so that this area is $1$. An affine map $T(x,y) = (kx, y/k)$ with $k>0$ has determinant $1$, so it preserves areas, maps lines to lines and preserves convexity. Hence $T$ maps the regular pentagon to a convex pentagon with the same property. The perimeter $p(k)$ of the image is continuous in $k$ and tends to infinity as $k \to\infty$ (some side has a nonzero horizontal component, which is multiplied by $k$), so $p(k)$ takes infinitely many different values. Congruent pentagons have equal perimeters, so we obtain infinitely many non-congruent pentagons with the property. ∎
